messages.subject: Meta-analysis (hierarchical) model chain tips
parts:
Hello,

I am fitting a hierarchical model to MRR data (for species where individual identification is not possible) from a number of different studies, and wanted to gauge opinions on the model structure below - any feedback/suggestions would be most helpful!

Separately, getting convergence in the individual studies is fine, but overall it is proving very problematic. I am running 8-32 chains, and have the issue whereby sometimes convergence is reached, but other times, either the log-probability parameter doesn't, and sometimes a number of the parameters do not converge. 

The stan code I am using is below, and the data file is attached. Any help with sorting this convergence issue would be helpful! 

Details of the model
We assume that on day 0, N of the organism are released into the wild. Efforts are made to recapture the organisms on days t>=1, and the decline in the numbers recaptured with time is used to infer mortality (this is typical of MRR experiments). The mean number recaptured on a given day, t,  can be shown to be well-approximated by the following (assuming the numbers recaptured on previous days is small relative to the overall release number):

lambda(t) = N * psi * e^(-mu * t) 

where psi is the probability of recapture of an individual mosquito on any given day, and mu is the rate of mortality, which is assumed to be independent of age. Our likelihood model that we choose to use is the negative binomial parameterised by its mean,lambda(t), and a dispersion parameter, kappa, to account for swarming/mass behaviour of the organism:

y(t) ~ NB(\lambda(t),kappa)

We have data from a number of individual MRR studies which we would like to combine in a manner that allows for individual heterogeneity in the studies. A natural choice here is to use a hierarchical model, we each of the parameters (psi,kappa,mu) in each study are derived from distributions that represent species-level characteristics. In particular we assign the following priors:

logit(psi) ~ N(m_psi,sigma_psi)
kappa ~ log-normal(p,r)
mu ~ gamma(a,b)

where the hyper-parameters themselves are assigned hyper-priors. 

data {
  int<lower=0> N; ## Total number of observations
  int<lower=0> K; ## Total number of studies
  int Y[N]; ## Vector of observations for the release
  int S[K]; ## Array of ints for the study lengths
  vector[N] t; ## Vector of time observations (days) 
  int Pos[K]; ## Array of the starting position of each dataset
  vector[K] RelNumber; ## Vector of the numbers released across each study
  } 


parameters {
  ## Study-specific parameters
  real<lower=0,upper=1> psi[K];
  real<lower=0,upper=1000> kappa[K];
  real<lower=0> mu[K];
  
  ## Overarching parameters
  real mPsi;
  real<lower=0> sigmaPsi;
  real p;
  real<lower=0> r;
  real<lower=0> a;
  real<lower=0> b;
} 

  
transformed parameters {
  real phi[K];
  for (i in 1:K)
  {
phi[i] <- logit(psi[i]);
  }
}
 
model {
  for (i in 1:K) {
  
real lambda[S[i]];
real R_times_psi;
R_times_psi <- RelNumber[i]*psi[i];
for (j in 1:S[i])
{
lambda[j] <- R_times_psi * exp(-mu[i] * t[Pos[i] + j - 1]);
Y[Pos[i] + j - 1] ~ neg_binomial_2(lambda[j]+1e-5 , kappa[i]);
}
}
  ## Individual study parameters
  for (i in 1:K)
  {
   phi[i] ~ normal(mPsi,sigmaPsi);
   kappa[i] ~ lognormal(p,r);
   mu[i] ~ gamma(a,b);
  }
  
  ## Overall study parameters
  a ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  b ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  mPsi ~ normal(0,10);
  sigmaPsi ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  p ~ normal(0,3);
  r ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
  
  ## Account for nonlinear transformation of psi
  for (i in 1:K)
  {
increment_log_prob(-log(fabs(psi[i]*(1-psi[i]))));
  }
}


Best,

Ben

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: Meta-analysis (hierarchical) model chain tips
parts:
Hi Ben,

I'm assuming that by "Separately, getting convergence in the individual studies is fine, but overall it is proving very problematic.", you mean that once you add hyperpriors for psi, mu and kappa, thinks fall apart. It would be useful if you could point out which parameters do not converge. Also, did you check for divergent iterations (see elsewhere on this list on how to do that in R)?

My first intuition is that study-level parameters mu and psi are going to be highly, positively correlated. The higher mortality rate mu, the fewer mosquitoes are predicted to be around, and thus, the higher the capture rate psi has to be. Any deviations from the exponential survival will be absorbed by the NB sampling error, mediated by kappa.

How much information do you have in your data? Your hyperpriors for mu, psi, and kappa are superweak, and may allow your model to wander. E.g., normal(0,10) for the meanof mu is far too wide; 99% of log-odds are between -5 and 5. You may want to try narrowing your hyperpriors, and see how the model behaves. If it's still aweful, there might be some problems with sampling efficiency related to the posterior geometry (I defer to others to comment on this).

Best,

Luc

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: Meta-analysis (hierarchical) model chain tips
parts:
Hi Ben,

I think your prior on psi is problematic.  Attached, generated via:

tp <- {mPsi<-rnorm(10^3, 0, 10); sigmaPsi <- rcauchy(10^3); phi <- rnorm(10^3, mPsi, abs(sigmaPsi)); list(mPsi, sigmaPsi, phi)}
pdf(file='/tmp/orly.pdf'); print(hist(plogis(tp[[3]]), breaks=100)); dev.off()

I also ran your model and noticed that it might help to use a kappa parameter with more mass near [-1,1] and maybe a transformed parameter for the actual kappa in neg_binomial_2.  In fact unless you really want infinite overdispersion to be possible, you might want a prior on the inverse of the overdispersion (but the current log-normal is also a little extreme).

Krzysztof
